items.title: E1. Oracle coverage
items.prompt: Compute oracle coverage for $p=0.25$ at $N=1,4,8,16$. Explain why the table does not describe a verifier.
items.answer:
*Solution.* Under independent attempts, no candidate is correct with probability $(1-p)^N$, so oracle coverage is $1-(1-p)^N$.

| $N$ | coverage |
|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.250000 |
| 4 | 0.683594 |
| 8 | 0.899887 |
| 16 | 0.989977 |

This is the probability that a correct candidate **exists**; calculating it needs no verifier at all. It would equal system accuracy under perfect selection. The table specifies no real verifier TPR/FPR and therefore does not predict which candidate will be selected.

items.title: E2. Non-uniform distractors
items.prompt: Modify the exact voting model so that two distractors are common and four are rare. Compare it with the uniform-distractor case.
items.answer:
*Solution.* Make the comparison concrete by keeping $p_{correct}=0.4$ and allocating the remaining 0.6 as `(0.20, 0.20, 0.05, 0.05, 0.05, 0.05)`; the uniform baseline has six distractors at 0.10. In the multinomial-composition enumeration, replace only the probability vector and keep the tie rule fixed.

| $N$ | unique mode, uniform | unique mode, skew | random tie, uniform | random tie, skew |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.400000 | 0.400000 | 0.400000 | 0.400000 |
| 3 | 0.352000 | 0.352000 | 0.472000 | 0.460000 |
| 5 | 0.509440 | 0.456640 | 0.595840 | 0.554380 |
| 9 | 0.671058 | 0.583120 | 0.737035 | 0.657549 |
| 17 | 0.856688 | 0.728538 | 0.889316 | 0.775702 |

Common distractors consolidate wrong votes and compete more often with the correct mode. Equal one-shot correctness therefore does not imply equal self-consistency gains.

items.title: E3. Noisy verifier
items.prompt: Plot the noisy-verifier curve through $N=64$ for TPR $=0.85$ and FPR $=0.10$. Identify diminishing returns.
items.answer:
*Solution.* Use the module scenario $p_{correct}=0.4$: independently accept a correct candidate with probability 0.85 and an incorrect one with 0.10; select uniformly among accepted candidates and fall back to a random generated candidate if none are accepted. Exact enumeration gives:

| $N$ | accuracy |
|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.400000 |
| 2 | 0.580000 |
| 4 | 0.752800 |
| 8 | 0.837403 |
| 16 | 0.849788 |
| 32 | 0.850000 |
| 64 | 0.850000 |

Gains diminish sharply around $N=8$. The limit is $q=0.4\cdot0.85/(0.4\cdot0.85+0.6\cdot0.10)=0.85$. Its equality to TPR is a numerical coincidence; the limit is correctness conditional on acceptance. §7 already provides a counterexample: TPR $=0.90$ gives a limit of $12/13$.

items.title: E4. FP8 KV
items.prompt: Recompute the KV table for 48 layers, KV width 512, and fp8 storage.
items.answer:
*Solution.* FP8 uses one byte per element, and K and V are stored separately:

$$M_{token}=2\cdot48\cdot512\cdot1=49152\ \text{bytes}=48\ \text{KiB}.$$

| Tokens | KV per request |
|---:|---:|
| 512 | 0.023438 GiB |
| 1,000 | 0.045776 GiB |
| 4,000 | 0.183105 GiB |
| 16,000 | 0.732422 GiB |
| 64,000 | 2.929688 GiB |

This is $128/48=2.667$ times smaller than the original 128 KiB/token scenario. It is payload only, excluding scales, alignment, allocator overhead, and runtime buffers.

items.title: E8. Unit tests as a verifier
items.prompt: Explain how a unit-test suite can be both more reliable than an LLM judge and still incomplete.
items.answer: *Solution.* With fixed inputs and a deterministic environment, a test reproducibly checks a stated requirement. Answer position and verbosity do not change its verdict, and a failure supplies a counterexample. A suite nevertheless checks only its recorded inputs and assertions. A program may overfit visible examples or violate uncovered edge cases, security requirements, or performance constraints. A nondeterministic environment can also make a test flaky. Passing therefore supports correctness within tested coverage; hidden cases, property tests, fuzzing, and review of the specification provide additional evidence.
